en: Dīgha Nikāya 2: The Discourse on the Fruits of Recluseship (Sāmaññaphala-sutta) 1. The Discussion with the King’s Ministers [The Buddha] was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Sanctuary. At that time, King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha, having mounted his state elephant and accompanied by a large retinue of ministers, set out from Rājagaha toward the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Sanctuary, to visit the Blessed One. Then the king’s chief minister, Abhaya, seeing King Ajātasattu from afar, spoke thus to him: “Sire, do not go to the recluse Gotama. For the recluse Gotama speaks in praise of abstention from killing, while you, sire, delight in killing. The recluse Gotama speaks in praise of abstention from taking what is not given, while you, sire, delight in taking what is not given. The recluse Gotama speaks in praise of celibacy, while you, sire, take pleasure in sexual intercourse. The recluse Gotama speaks in praise of abstaining from false speech, while you, sire, delight in speaking falsehoods. The recluse Gotama speaks in praise of abstaining from fermented and distilled liquors, which are the basis for negligence, while you, sire, delight in drinking fermented and distilled liquors. Sire, do not go to the recluse Gotama. A second time, and a third time, King Ajātasattu spoke thus to his chief minister Abhaya: “Abhaya, do not say such things. Do not disparage the recluse Gotama. The recluse Gotama is a worthy person, a perfectly awakened one, fully enlightened. It would be good for me to see such a worthy person. Then King Ajātasattu, having dismissed his retinue of ministers, proceeded alone toward the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Sanctuary, to visit the Blessed One. He went as far as the path was passable for carriages and then continued on foot. He approached the Blessed One, exchanged greetings with him, and sat down to one side. As he sat there, King Ajātasattu said this to the Blessed One:

“Master Gotama, I have heard this: ‘The recluse Gotama knows the way to the state of a king. Now, Master Gotama, does the recluse Gotama know the way to the state of a king? “I know the way to the state of a king, great king, and I also know the way to the higher states than that of a king. “Then, Master Gotama, please teach me the way to the state of a king. “Great king, when a king is endowed with five qualities, he is capable of ruling over his own kingdom and is also fit to invade the territory of another king. What five? Here, great king, a king is well-born on both sides, of pure descent back through seven generations, unblemished and of irreproachable birth. Great king, when a king is endowed with this first quality, he is capable of ruling over his own kingdom and is also fit to invade the territory of another king. Furthermore, great king, a king is wealthy, with abundant treasure and granaries. Great king, when a king is endowed with this second quality... Furthermore, great king, a king possesses a large army consisting of four divisions: elephants, cavalry, chariots, and infantry. Great king, when a king is endowed with this third quality... Furthermore, great king, a king has a wise and sagacious counselor who knows the right time to speak and the wrong time to speak, who knows the meaning of what is said and who is capable of deliberating on matters of policy. Great king, when a king is endowed with this fourth quality... Furthermore, great king, a king has a brave and heroic general who is skilled in battle and capable of leading the army. Great king, when a king is endowed with this fifth quality, he is capable of ruling over his own kingdom and is also fit to invade the territory of another king. “Master Gotama, it is wonderful, it is marvelous how the recluse Gotama knows the way to the state of a king, and also the way to the higher states than that of a king. Master Gotama, I am now a king endowed with these five qualities. Master Gotama, I am well-born on both sides, of pure descent back through seven generations, unblemished and of irreproachable birth. I am wealthy, with abundant treasure and granaries. I possess a large army consisting of four divisions. I have a wise and sagacious counselor who knows the right time to speak and the wrong time to speak, who knows the meaning of what is said and who is capable of deliberating on matters of policy. And I have a brave and heroic general who is skilled in battle and capable of leading the army. Master Gotama, I am now a king endowed with these five qualities. “Great king, when a king is endowed with these five qualities, he is capable of ruling over his own kingdom and is also fit to invade the territory of another king. But, great king, a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin rāja), a righteous king who rules by the Dhamma, is endowed with seven treasures and four kinds of success (iddhi). What seven? Here, great king, a wheel-turning monarch possesses the Wheel Treasure, the Elephant Treasure, the Horse Treasure, the Jewel Treasure, the Woman Treasure, the Householder Treasure, and the Counselor Treasure as the seventh. These are the seven treasures he possesses. And what, great king, are the four kinds of success? Here, great king, a wheel-turning monarch is successful in terms of longevity, beauty, happiness, and power. These are the four kinds of success he possesses. A wheel-turning monarch, great king, is endowed with these seven treasures and four kinds of success. “It is wonderful, Master Gotama, it is marvelous how the recluse Gotama knows the way to the state of a king, and also the way to the higher states than that of a king. Master Gotama, I am now a king endowed with these five qualities. Master Gotama, I am well-born on both sides... [as above] ...I have a brave and heroic general... Master Gotama, I am now a king endowed with these five qualities. But, Master Gotama, I do not possess the seven treasures or the four kinds of success of a wheel-turning monarch. Therefore, Master Gotama, I wish to go forth under the Blessed One, to receive the full ordination. “Great king, if you were to go forth under me, would you be able to abandon the five lower fetters? “Master Gotama, I am a busy man, with much to do. How could I abandon the five lower fetters? “Great king, if you were to go forth under me, would you be able to abandon the five hindrances? “Master Gotama, I am a busy man, with much to do. How could I abandon the five hindrances? “Great king, if you were to go forth under me, would you be able to practice the four foundations of mindfulness? “Master Gotama, I am a busy man, with much to do. How could I practice the four foundations of mindfulness? “Great king, if you were to go forth under me, would you be able to practice the four right efforts? “Master Gotama, I am a busy man, with much to do. How could I practice the four right efforts? “Great king, if you were to go forth under me, would you be able to practice the four bases of psychic power? “Master Gotama, I am a busy man, with much to do. How could I practice the four bases of psychic power? “Great king, if you were to go forth under me, would you be able to practice the five faculties? “Master Gotama, I am a busy man, with much to do. How could I practice the five faculties? “Great king, if you were to go forth under me, would you be able to practice the five powers? “Master Gotama, I am a busy man, with much to do. How could I practice the five powers?

“Great king, if you were to go forth under me, would you be able to practice the seven factors of enlightenment? “Master Gotama, I am a busy man, with much to do. How could I practice the seven factors of enlightenment? “Great king, if you were to go forth under me, would you be able to practice the Noble Eightfold Path? “Master Gotama, I am a busy man, with much to do. How could I practice the Noble Eightfold Path? “Great king, if you were to go forth under me, would you be able to abandon the ten unwholesome courses of action? “Master Gotama, I am a busy man, with much to do. How could I abandon the ten unwholesome courses of action? “Great king, if you were to go forth under me, would you be able to practice the ten wholesome courses of action? “Master Gotama, I am a busy man, with much to do. How could I practice the ten wholesome courses of action? “Great king, if you were to go forth under me, would you be able to abandon the sixty-two speculative views? “Master Gotama, I am a busy man, with much to do. How
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in Jīvaka Komārabhacca’s mango grove, together with a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus, numbering twelve hundred and fifty bhikkhus.
Now on that occasion, it was the Uposatha day of the fifteenth, and King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha...
On the full-moon night of the Komudi Cātumāsini festival, the King was seated on the upper terrace of his magnificent palace, surrounded by his ministers.
Then, on that Uposatha day, King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha uttered this inspired exclamation:

"How delightful indeed, sirs, is this moonlit night! How beautiful indeed, sirs, is this moonlit night! How worthy of being seen indeed, sirs, is this moonlit night! How serene indeed, sirs, is this moonlit night! How auspicious indeed, sirs, is this moonlit night!"
“Whom indeed should we attend upon today, whether a recluse or a brahmin, so that our minds might find confidence through attending upon him?
When this was said, a certain royal minister said to King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha:

“Your Majesty, this Pūraṇa Kassapa is a leader of an order, a leader of a group, a teacher of a group; he is renowned and famous, a founder of a sect, esteemed as holy by many people, long-ordained, of long standing, advanced in years, and come to the last stage of life.”
“Let Your Majesty attend upon Pūraṇa Kassapa;
perhaps, by attending upon Pūraṇa Kassapa, Your Majesty’s mind will find confidence.
When this was said, King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha remained silent.
Another royal minister also said this to King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha:

“Sire, this Makkhali Gosāla is a leader of a community, a chief of a group, and a teacher of a school; he is well-known, famous, a founder of a sect, highly esteemed by the multitude, long-ordained, of ancient standing, advanced in years, and come to the end of his life’s journey.
Let Your Majesty wait upon Makkhali Gosāla.”
“Perhaps, if Your Majesty were to attend upon Makkhali Gosāla, his mind might become serene.
When this was said, King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha remained silent.
Then another royal minister said this to King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha:

“Sire, this Ajita Kesakambala is the head of an order, the leader of a group, the teacher of a school; he is renowned and famous, an acknowledged founder of a sect, esteemed by many as a holy man, long-ordained, of long standing, advanced in years, and come to the last stage of life.
Let the King pay court to Ajita Kesakambala;
perhaps, while paying court to Ajita Kesakambala, the King’s mind might find confidence.”
When this was said, King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha became silent.
Then a certain royal minister said this to King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha:

"Sire, this Pakudha Kaccāyana is a leader of a community, a leader of a group, a teacher of a group; he is well-known and famous, a founder of a sect esteemed as virtuous by the many, long-veteran in the religious life, advanced in years, and arrived at old age."
“Let Your Majesty pay homage to Pakudha Kaccāyana.
Perhaps, by paying homage to Pakudha Kaccāyana, Your Majesty’s mind might find confidence.
When this was said, Ajātasattu Vedehiputta, the King of Magadha, remained silent.
Another royal minister also said this to King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha:

"Sire, this Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta is a leader of an assembly, a chief of a group, and a teacher of a school; he is renowned and famous, an established founder of a sect, highly esteemed by the multitude, long-veteran in the religious life, advanced in years, and arrived at the final stage of life.
Let Your Majesty attend upon this Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta."
"Perhaps, if Your Majesty were to attend upon Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta, your mind might find confidence.
When this was said, King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha remained silent.
Then another royal minister said this to King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha:

“Your Majesty, this Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta is the head of an order, the head of a group, the teacher of a group; he is well-known, famous, a founder of a sect, highly esteemed by the multitude, long-ordained, senior, advanced in years, and come to the last stage of life.
May Your Majesty pay homage to this Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta.
Perhaps, by paying homage to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, Your Majesty’s heart may find confidence.”
When this was said, King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha became silent.
Now at that time, Jīvaka Komārabhacca was sitting silently not far from King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha.
Then King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha said this to Jīvaka Komārabhacca:
"But you, my dear Jīvaka, why are you silent?
"Your Majesty, this Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One, is staying in our mango grove together with a great community of monks, numbering twelve hundred and fifty monks."
Furthermore, this auspicious report concerning that Blessed One has spread abroad: “Such indeed is that Blessed One:

the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Well-Gone, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed Leader of persons to be tamed, the Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Let the King pay homage to that Blessed One.
“Perhaps, sire, as you attend upon the Blessed One, your mind might find confidence.
“In that case, my dear Jīvaka, have the elephant-vehicles prepared,” said the King.
“Very well, sire,” replied Jīvaka Komārabhacca to Ajātasattu Vedehiputta, the King of Magadha.
Having given his consent, he had about five hundred female elephants prepared, including a royal elephant fit for the king’s mounting,
and announced to King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha:
“Your Majesty, the elephant mounts have been prepared.”
"Now, do as you deem fit.
Then King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha, having had five hundred female elephants each mounted by a woman and having himself ascended his royal state elephant,
set out from Rājagaha with great royal splendor while torches were being carried before him.
He set out for Jīvaka Komārabhacca’s mango grove.
Then, not far from the mango grove, King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha was seized by fear, he was struck with trepidation, and his hair stood on end.
Thereupon, King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha, frightened, agitated, and with his hair standing on end, said this to Jīvaka Komārabhacca:
“Am I not being deceived by you, dear Jīvaka?
Am I not being cheated by you, dear Jīvaka?
Are you not handing me over to my enemies, dear Jīvaka?”
"How is it possible that for such a great community of monks—twelve hundred and fifty monks in all—there will be neither the sound of sneezing, nor the sound of coughing, nor any noise at all?
"Do not fear, Great King, do not fear, Great King.
I am not deceiving you, O Lord."
“I do not deceive you, Your Majesty;
I do not hand you over to your enemies.
Come forward, Great King! Come forward, Great King! These lamps are burning in the assembly hall.”
3. The Question on the Fruits of the Ascetic Life.

Then King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha, having traveled by elephant as far as the ground was passable for an elephant, dismounted from the elephant and approached the door of the circular pavilion on foot; having approached, he...
He said this to Jīvaka Komārabhacca:
“But where, friend Jīvaka, is the Blessed One?
“That, Great King, is the Blessed One;”
“Great King, this Blessed One is seated leaning against the middle pillar, facing eastward, with the community of monks before him.
Then King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha approached the Blessed One; having approached, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha surveyed the silent community of monks and, like a lake that is perfectly serene, uttered this inspired exclamation:
“May Prince Udayabhadda be endowed with this same peace that the Saṅgha of bhikkhus is now endowed with.
“You have come, Great King, as was dear to you.
“Venerable sir, Prince Udayabhadda is dear to me.”
“By this same peace, venerable sir, may Prince Udayabhadda be endowed, as the Saṅgha of bhikkhus is now endowed with that peace.
Then King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha, having paid homage to the Blessed One and extended his joined palms in salutation toward the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha addressed the Blessed One thus:
“Venerable sir, I would ask the Blessed One about a certain matter,
if the Blessed One would grant me the opportunity for an answer to my question.
“Ask, great king, whatever you desire,” [the Blessed One replied].
“Venerable sir, just as there are these various crafts and professions,
namely: elephant-riders, horse-riders, charioteers, archers, standard-bearers, banner-carriers, messengers, high-born princes, noble youths, great heroes, brave men, shield-bearers, slaves’ sons,
cooks, barbers, bath-attendants, chefs, garland-makers, dyers, weavers, basket-makers, potters, and accountants...”
Grapes, or whatever other various fields of craft there may be of this kind— they enjoy the visible fruit of their craft in this very life;

by means of that, they bring happiness and satisfaction to themselves, they bring happiness and satisfaction to their mother and father, and they bring happiness and satisfaction to their children and wives.

They satisfy them; they bring happiness and satisfaction to their friends and companions; and they establish among recluses and brahmins a lofty offering that leads to heaven, has a happy result, and conduces to rebirth in the celestial realms.
Is it possible, venerable sir, to point out such a fruit of recluseship that is visible here and now, directly evident?”
“Do you recall, Great King, having asked this question of other ascetics and brahmins?
“I do recall, venerable sir, having asked this question of other ascetics and brahmins.
“But how, Great King, did they answer it? If it is not troublesome for you, please speak.”
“It is not burdensome for me, Bhante, to sit where the Blessed One is seated, or where one like the Blessed One is seated.
“In that case, Great King, speak,” [the Blessed One said].
3.1. The Refutation of Pūraṇa Kassapa’s Doctrine
“On one occasion, venerable sir, I approached Pūraṇa Kassapa; having approached, I exchanged greetings with Pūraṇa Kassapa.
When we had concluded our courteous and amiable conversation, I sat down to one side. Seated to one side, venerable sir, I said this to Pūraṇa Kassapa:
‘Venerable Kassapa, as for these various crafts and occupations—’”
Namely: elephant-riders, horse-riders, chariot-warriors, archers, standard-bearers, banner-carriers, messengers, high-born nobles, princes,
intrepid warriors, great champions, heroes, shieldmen, sons of slave-girls, cooks, barbers, bath-attendants,
chefs, garland-makers, dyers, weavers, basket-makers, potters, accountants, and scribes, or whatever others there may be.
These various fields of craft, when practiced in this way, provide their practitioners with visible fruits of their craft in this very life.

By means of that, they bring happiness and satisfaction to themselves; they bring happiness and satisfaction to their mother and father; they bring happiness and satisfaction to their wife and children;
they bring happiness and satisfaction to their friends and colleagues; and they establish a lofty sacrificial gift for ascetics and brahmins.
“Leading to heaven, resulting in happiness, and conducive to rebirth in heaven.
Is it possible, Master Kassapa, to point out such a fruit of recluseship that is visible here and now, directly experienced?
When this was said, venerable sir, Pūraṇa Kassapa spoke to me as follows:
‘For one who acts, O Great King, or causes another to act; who cuts, or causes another to cut; who cooks, or causes another to cook;
who grieves, or causes another to grieve; who exerts himself, or causes another to exert himself; who trembles, or causes another to tremble; who takes life, or causes another to take life;
who takes what is not given, or causes another to take it; who breaks into a dwelling, or carries off plunder; who commits burglary, or lies in ambush—’
For one who goes to another's wife, for one who speaks falsely, no evil is committed by doing so. Even if, with a wheel whose edge is as sharp as a razor,
one were to reduce all living beings on this earth to a single heap of flesh, a single mass of flesh, there would be no evil resulting from that,
nor would there be any consequence of evil.

‘If one were to go along the southern bank of the Ganges, killing and causing to kill, mutilating and causing to mutilate, torturing and causing to torture, there would be no evil on that account, nor would there be any arrival of evil.

And if one were to go along the northern bank of the Ganges, giving and causing to give, sacrificing and causing to sacrifice, there would be no merit on that account, nor would there be any arrival of merit.
There is no merit, and there is no arrival of merit, from giving, self-control, restraint, or speaking the truth.’”
"Thus, venerable sir, when I asked Pūraṇa Kassapa about the fruit of recluseship visible here and now, he explained non-action to me. Just as if, venerable sir,
one asked about a mango and answered about a breadfruit tree, or asked about a breadfruit tree and answered about a mango— just so, venerable sir,
when I asked Pūraṇa Kassapa about the fruit of recluseship visible here and now, he explained non-action to me."
Then, Bhante, it occurred to me:
“How could one such as I think that a recluse or a brahmin living within his realm should be disparaged?
Thus, Bhante, I neither approved nor rejected what Pūraṇa Kassapa had said.
Without approving, without rejecting, being displeased yet not uttering words of displeasure, neither grasping at nor casting aside those very words, I rose from my seat and departed.
3.2. The Doctrine of Makkhali Gosāla On one occasion, venerable sir, I approached Makkhali Gosāla; having approached, I exchanged greetings with Makkhali Gosāla.
Having exchanged greetings and pleasantries, I sat down to one side. Seated there, venerable sir, I said to Makkhali Gosāla:
“Master Gosāla, regarding these various crafts and professions...
[as before] ...is it possible, Master Gosāla, to point out a fruit of recluseship that is visible here and now, directly experienced?”
When this was said, venerable sir, Makkhali Gosāla said this to me:
“Great King, there is no cause, there is no condition for the defilement of beings; beings are defiled without cause or condition.
There is no cause, there is no condition for the purification of beings...”
"Beings are purified without cause or condition.
There is no personal effort, no external effort, no human effort, no power, no energy, no human strength, and no human exertion.

All beings, all living things, all creatures, and all souls are powerless, weak, and devoid of energy; they are transformed by destiny, chance, and inherent nature, and it is within the six classes of birth that they experience pleasure and pain."
Now, there are these fourteen hundred thousand principal wombs,
sixty-six hundred, five hundred actions, five actions, three actions, action and half-action, sixty-two paths, sixty-two intermediate eons,
six classes of rebirth, eight stages of man, four hundred and ninety-nine modes of livelihood, and four hundred and ninety-nine [types of] ascetics.
There are four hundred and ninety-nine wandering ascetics, two hundred Nāga abodes, three hundred faculties, thirty hells,
thirty-six elements of dust, seven wombs of percipient beings, seven wombs of non-percipient beings,
seven wombs of Nigaṇṭhas, seven gods, seven humans, seven Piśācas, seven lakes, seven whirlpools, seven hundred whirlpools, and seven precipices.
Seven hundred precipices, seven dreams, seven hundred dreams, and eighty-four thousand great aeons—having run on and wandered through these, both fools and the wise will make an end of suffering.

In this regard, there is no such thing as thinking, "By means of this virtue, or vow, or austerity, or holy life, I shall ripen unripened karma, or I shall, by repeatedly encountering ripened karma, bring it to an end. Indeed, there is nothing of the sort.
‘Happiness and suffering are measured out; saṃsāra is limited and has its bounds fixed. There is no decrease and no increase, no excess and no deficiency.
Just as a ball of thread, when thrown, unwinds only until it is exhausted, even so both the fool and the wise, having run their course and wandered through saṃsāra, will make an end of suffering.’”
"Thus, venerable sir, when I asked Makkhali Gosāla about the fruit of recluseship visible here and now, he explained purification through the cycle of rebirth. Just as if, venerable sir,
one asked about a mango and he answered about a breadfruit tree, or asked about a breadfruit tree and he answered about a mango— even so, venerable sir,
when I asked Makkhali Gosāla about the fruit of recluseship visible here and now, he explained purification through the cycle of rebirth."
Then, Bhante, it occurred to me:
"How could one such as I think that a recluse or a brahmin living within my realm should be disparaged?
Thus, Bhante, I neither rejoiced in Makkhali Gosāla’s speech nor did I reject it.

Without accepting it and without rejecting it, being dissatisfied yet refraining from uttering words of dissatisfaction, neither upholding nor discarding that very statement, I rose from my seat and departed.
3.3. The Doctrine of Ajita Kesakambala On one occasion, venerable sir, I approached Ajita Kesakambala; having approached him, I exchanged greetings with Ajita Kesakambala.
Having exchanged greetings and pleasantries, I sat down to one side. Seated to one side, venerable sir, I said to Ajita Kesakambala:
“Master Ajita, just as these various crafts and professions...
[as before] ...is it possible, Master Ajita, to point out a fruit of the ascetic life that is visible here and now, directly experienced?”
When this was said, Bhante, Ajita Kesakambala said this to me:
“Great King, there is no giving, there is no sacrifice, there is no offering;
there is no fruit or result of deeds well done or ill done; there is no this world, there is no other world; there is no mother, there is no father.”

"There are no beings who are spontaneously born; there are no recluses or brahmins in the world who have attained the right path and practiced rightly, who, having realized this world and the other world for themselves through direct knowledge, make them known.
This person consists of the four great elements; when he dies, earth returns to the earth-body and follows it."
The water element enters and goes toward the body of water; the fire element enters and goes toward the body of fire;
the air element enters and goes toward the body of air; space passes over to the sense faculties.
Four men, with a bier as the fifth, carry away the dead.
As long as the footprints leading to the cremation ground are visible,
the bones turn pigeon-colored, and the offerings vanish;
thus, this so-called "giving" is merely established by convention.
"Whatever proponents of existence speak, their talk is empty and false.
Both fools and the wise, with the breakup of the body, are cut off and perish; they do not exist after death.
Thus, Bhante, when Ajita Kesakambala was asked about the fruit of recluseship visible here and now, he explained it as annihilationism.
"Venerable sir, just as if one asked about a mango might answer about a breadfruit, or as if one asked about a breadfruit might answer about a mango—
even so, venerable sir, when Ajita Kesakambala was asked by me about the visible fruit of recluseship, he explained annihilation to me. Then, venerable sir, this occurred to me:"
"How indeed could one such as I think that a recluse or a brahmin living within my realm should be disparaged?
Venerable sir, I neither approved nor rejected what Ajita Kesakambala had said.
Without approving or rejecting it, being dissatisfied yet not uttering words of dissatisfaction, and neither upholding nor casting aside those very words, I rose from my seat and departed.
3.4. The Doctrine of Pakudha Kaccāyana "Once, venerable sir, I approached where Pakudha Kaccāyana was staying. Having approached, I exchanged greetings with Pakudha Kaccāyana.
When we had concluded our polite and courteous conversation, I sat down to one side. Seated to one side, venerable sir, I said this to Pakudha Kaccāyana:"
"But how is it, Master Kaccāyana, with these various crafts and occupations...
[as before] ...is it possible, Master Kaccāyana, to point out a fruit of recluseship that is visible here and now, directly experienced?
When this was said, venerable sir, Pakudha Kaccāyana spoke to me thus:
“Great King, there are these seven bodies that are unmade, not fashioned by a maker, uncreated, not created by a creator, barren, fixed like a mountain peak, standing firm like a pillar.
They do not move, they do not change, they do not obstruct one another, and they are incapable of bringing about each other’s pleasure, pain, or both pleasure and pain.
What are the seven? [The rest of the passage follows.]”
The earth-body, the water-body, the fire-body, the air-body, pleasure, pain, and the living being as the seventh— these seven bodies are uncreated,
not fashioned by a creator, unmade, not made by another, barren, fixed like a mountain peak, standing firm like a pillar.
They do not move, they do not change, they do not obstruct one another, and they are incapable of bringing about the pleasure, the pain, or both the pleasure and pain of one another.
"In that regard, there is no killer nor one who causes killing, no hearer nor one who causes hearing, no cognizer nor one who causes cognition.
Even when someone cuts off a head with a sharp sword, no one deprives anyone of life;
rather, the sword merely passes through the opening between the seven bodies."
"In this way, venerable sir, when I asked Pakudha Kaccāyana about the visible fruit of recluseship, he answered one thing while asking about another. Just as if, venerable sir,
one asked about a mango and he were to answer about a breadfruit tree, or asked about a breadfruit tree and he were to answer about a mango— just so, venerable sir,
when I asked Pakudha Kaccāyana about the visible fruit of recluseship, he answered me with something else."
Then, Bhante, it occurred to me:
"How could one such as I think that a recluse or a brahmin living within his realm should be censured?
Thus, Bhante, I neither approved nor rejected what Pakudha Kaccāyana had said.
Without approving, without rejecting, being displeased, yet not uttering words of displeasure, neither grasping nor disparaging those very words, I rose from my seat and departed.
3.5. The Doctrine of Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta On one occasion, venerable sir, I approached the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta; having approached, I exchanged greetings with the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta.
Having exchanged polite and courteous greetings, I sat down to one side. Seated to one side, venerable sir, I said to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta:
“Master Aggivessana, just as there are these various fields of craft...
[as before] ...is it possible, Master Aggivessana, to point out a fruit of recluseship that is visible here and now, directly experienced?”
When this was said, venerable sir, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta said this to me:
“In this case, great king, a Nigaṇṭha is restrained by the fourfold restraint.
And how, great king, is a Nigaṇṭha restrained by the fourfold restraint?”

In this case, Great King, a Nigaṇṭha is one who has restrained himself from all water [of evil], is devoted to all water [of virtue], has shaken off all water [of defilement], and has touched all water [of purity].
It is in this way, Great King, that a Nigaṇṭha is restrained by the fourfold restraint.
And when, Great King, a Nigaṇṭha is thus restrained by the fourfold restraint...
“Great King, this is called a Nigaṇṭha who has reached the goal, who is self-controlled, and who is established in himself.
In this way, Bhante, when I asked the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta about the fruit of recluseship visible here and now, he explained the fourfold restraint.
It was as if, Bhante, one asked about a mango and he answered about a breadfruit tree, or asked about a breadfruit tree and he answered about a mango.
"In the same way, venerable sir, when the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta was asked about the fruit of recluseship visible here and now, he explained it as the fourfold restraint.
Then, venerable sir, this occurred to me:
‘How indeed could one like me think that a recluse or brahmin living within his realm should be disparaged?’"
"Thus, venerable sir, I neither approved nor rejected the statement of Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta.
Without approving or rejecting it, being dissatisfied yet not uttering words of dissatisfaction, neither upholding nor casting aside those very words, I rose from my seat and departed.
3.6. The Doctrine of Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta"
“On one occasion, venerable sir, I approached Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta; having approached, I exchanged greetings with Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta.
When we had concluded our polite and courteous conversation, I sat down to one side. Sitting there, venerable sir, I said to Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta:
‘Now, Master Sañjaya, regarding these various crafts and professions...’”
“Is it possible, Master Sañjaya, to point out a fruit of recluseship that is visible here and now in this very life?
When this was said, venerable sir, Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta said this to me:
“If you ask me, ‘Is there another world? and if I were to hold that ‘there is another world,’ then I would answer you, ‘There is another world.’”
"Thus it is for me," I do not say; "in that way it is for me," I do not say; "otherwise it is for me," I do not say;
"it is not for me," I do not say; "it is not not for me," I do not say. "There is no other world... [and so on] "...there both is and is not another world... [and so on].
There neither is nor is not a world beyond …pe… there are beings of spontaneous birth …pe… there are no beings of spontaneous birth …pe…
"There both are and are not beings of spontaneous birth" ...
"it is neither that there are nor that there are not beings of spontaneous birth" ...
"there is fruit and result of deeds well done and ill done" ... [and so forth].

There is no fruit or result of good and evil deeds … [and so on] … there both is and is not a fruit or result of good and evil deeds … [and so on] … neither is there nor is there not a fruit or result of good and evil deeds … [and so on].
“The Tathāgata exists after death … [or] the Tathāgata does not exist after death … [or] the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death …” and so forth.
"If you ask me, 'Does the Tathāgata neither exist nor not exist after death?'—
if I held that 'the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death,' then I would declare to you: 'The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.'"
‘It is thus for me,’ said Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta, ‘nor is it otherwise for me, nor is it both thus and otherwise for me, nor is it neither thus nor otherwise for me.

In this way, Bhante, when questioned about the fruit of recluseship visible here and now, Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta gave an evasive answer. Just as if, Bhante, one asked about a mango would answer about a breadfruit, or one asked about a breadfruit would answer about a mango; so too did Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta, when questioned about the fruit of recluseship visible here and now, give an evasive answer.
“In the same way, Bhante, when Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta was asked about the fruit of recluseship visible here and now, he gave an evasive answer.
Then, Bhante, it occurred to me:
‘This man is the most foolish and the most deluded among all these recluses and brahmins.’”
"How could he, when asked about the fruit of recluseship that is visible here and now, give an evasive answer?
Then, venerable sir, this occurred to me:
"How could one such as I think it right to disparage a recluse or a brahmin living within my realm?"
Thus, venerable sir, I neither approved nor rejected the statement of Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta.
Without approving or rejecting it, being dissatisfied yet not uttering words of dissatisfaction, neither upholding nor casting aside that very speech, I rose from my seat and departed.
4. The Fruit of the Ascetic Life.
4.1. The First Fruit of the Homeless Life Visible Here and Now “Venerable sir, I ask the Blessed One this:
‘Now, venerable sir, as to these various crafts and occupations—’”

That is to say: elephant riders, cavalrymen, chariot warriors, archers, standard-bearers, banner-carriers, messengers, high-born nobles, princes, intrepid warriors, great heroes, brave men, shield-bearers, sons of slaves, cooks, barbers, bath-attendants, chefs, garland-makers, dyers, weavers, basket-makers, potters, accountants, and scribes;
or whatever other various fields of craft there may be of this kind—they [attain] the visible fruit in this very life.
They live off the fruits of their craft; by means of that,
they bring happiness and satisfaction to themselves, they bring happiness and satisfaction to their mother and father, they bring happiness and satisfaction to their children and wife,
they bring happiness and satisfaction to their friends and companions, and they establish a lofty sacrificial offering for ascetics and brahmins.
“Is it possible, Bhante, to point out in this very life a fruit of recluseship that is visible here and now, leading to heaven, with a happy result, and conducive to rebirth in heaven?
“It is possible, Great King.”
"In that case, Great King, I shall question you about this very matter. Answer it as you see fit.
What do you think, Great King?
Suppose here you had a man who was a slave and laborer—rising before you, retiring after you, obedient to whatever needs to be done, acting agreeably, speaking kindly, and looking to your face."
It would occur to him:
"How wonderful, indeed! How marvelous, indeed! Such is the course of merit, such is the fruition of merit.
For this King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha is a human being, and I too am a human being."
For this King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha, endowed and possessed of the five cords of sensual pleasure, sports as if he were a god.
Yet I am his slave and laborer—rising before him and retiring after him, obedient to his every command, acting with kindness, speaking pleasantly, looking to his face.
Oh, that I might perform meritorious deeds!
‘What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness?
After some time, he might shave off his hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness.
Having thus gone forth, he would dwell restrained in body, restrained in speech, and restrained in mind; content with nothing more than food and clothing, he would delight in solitude.
If those men were to report to you thus: "Truly, Your Majesty,

you should know that the man who was your slave and laborer— rising before you, retiring after you, obedient to your every command, agreeable in conduct, speaking kindly, and looking to your face— that man, Sire,
has shaved off his hair and beard, donned saffron robes, and gone forth from the home life into homelessness."
“Having thus gone forth, he dwells restrained in body, restrained in speech, and restrained in mind; he is content with mere food and clothing, and delights in seclusion.
Would you then say:
“Come, sir, let that man be my slave and laborer again—one who rises before me, retires after me, is obedient to my every command, behaves agreeably, speaks kindly, and looks to my face”?
“Certainly not, Bhante. On the contrary,
we ourselves would pay homage to him, rise up for him, invite him to a seat,
and would also offer him robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.”
“We would provide him with righteous protection, defense, and guardianship.
“What do you think, great king:
if this were so, would there be a visible fruit of recluseship, or not?”
“Surely, Bhante, when this is so, there is a visible fruit of recluseship in this very life.
“This, Great King, is the first visible fruit of recluseship in this very life that has been declared by me to you.
4.2. The Second Fruit of Recluseship Visible in This Life.
“But, venerable sir, is it possible to point out another fruit of recluseship, visible here and now, of a similar kind?
“It is possible, great king.
Therefore, great king, I shall question you about this very matter. Answer as you see fit.”
"What do you think, Great King?
Suppose here you had a man who was a farmer, a householder, a laborer, and one who increased his wealth.
It would occur to him thus:"
‘It is wonderful indeed, sir! It is marvelous indeed, sir! Such is the destination of merit, such is the fruition of merit!
For this King Māgadha Ajātasattu Vedehiputta is a human being, and I too am a human being.
Yet this King Māgadha Ajātasattu Vedehiputta, endowed and possessed of the five strands of sensual pleasure, enjoys himself as if he were a god.’
"But I am his farmer, a householder, a laborer who increases his wealth.
It would indeed be right for me to perform meritorious deeds.
What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, don saffron robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness?"
Then, at a later time, having abandoned either a small or a great mass of wealth,
and having abandoned either a small or a great circle of kinsmen, he might shave off his hair and beard,
don saffron robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness.
Having thus gone forth, he should dwell restrained in body, restrained in speech, and restrained in mind; content with the mere necessities of food and clothing, and delighting in solitude.
If those men were to report this to you, saying:
"Sire, you should know that the man who was your farmer, a householder, a doer of work, and an increaser of wealth..."
“Having shaved off his hair and beard and donned saffron robes, he has gone forth from the home life into homelessness.
Having thus gone forth, he dwells restrained in body, restrained in speech, and restrained in mind; he is content with mere food and clothing, and delights in seclusion.
Would you then say this?
“‘Sir, let that man come back to me; let him once again be a farmer, a householder, a doer of work, and a builder of wealth.
‘Certainly not, Bhante.
On the contrary, we ourselves would pay homage to him, rise up for him, and invite him to a seat.’”
“We would even invite him with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick;
we would also provide him with righteous protection, defense, and guard.
“What do you think, Great King?”
“If this is so, does the fruit of recluseship exist as something visible here and now, or not?
“Certainly, venerable sir, if this is so, the fruit of recluseship exists as something visible here and now.
“This, great king, is the second fruit of recluseship that I have declared to you as visible here and now in this very life.”

4.3. A More Exalted Fruit of Recluseship “But, venerable sir, is it possible to point out another fruit of recluseship visible here and now, more excellent and sublime than these fruits of recluseship visible here and now?
“It is possible, great king.”
"In that case, great king, listen and pay close attention; I shall speak.
"Yes, venerable sir," the Magadhan King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:

“Here, Great King, a Tathāgata arises in the world, an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Well-Gone One, a knower of the worlds, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
Having realized this world—with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans—by his own direct knowledge, he makes it known.”
He teaches the Dhamma that is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end, both in meaning and in phrasing; he proclaims the holy life, entirely complete and pure.
A householder, or a householder’s son, or one born into some other family, hears that Dhamma.
Having heard that Dhamma, he gains faith in the Tathāgata.
Endowed with that attainment of faith, he reflects thus:
"Household life is crowded and dusty; going forth is open air.
It is not easy for one dwelling at home to practice the holy life in its full perfection, complete purity, and total polish."
‘What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, don saffron robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness?
Then, at a later time, having abandoned a small or large mass of wealth,
and having abandoned a small or large circle of relatives, he shaves off his hair and beard.
Having clothed himself in saffron-colored robes, he goes forth from the household life into homelessness.

Having thus gone forth, he dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, perfected in conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and training himself by undertaking the rules of training; he is endowed with bodily and verbal action that is well-restrained.
One who is skilled, pure in livelihood, perfected in virtue, guarded in the doors of the sense faculties, endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension, and contented.
4.3.1. Virtue. 4.3.1.1. The Shorter Code of Virtue.
And how, Great King, is a bhikkhu accomplished in virtue?

Here, Great King, a bhikkhu, having abandoned the taking of life, abstains from taking life. Laying aside the rod and laying aside the weapon, being modest and compassionate, he dwells sympathetic toward the welfare of all living beings.
This, too, is his virtue.
Having abandoned taking what is not given, he abstains from taking what is not given; he takes only what is given, expects only what is given, and dwells with a heart free from theft and pure.
This too is part of his virtue.
Having abandoned unchastity, he lives a life of chastity; he dwells apart and abstains from the vulgar practice of sexual intercourse.
This too pertains to his virtue:
having abandoned false speech, he abstains from false speech; he is a speaker of truth, devoted to truth, trustworthy, reliable, and not a deceiver of the world.
This too pertains to his virtue.
Having abandoned malicious speech, he abstains from malicious speech.

Having heard something here, he does not repeat it elsewhere for the purpose of dividing these people; nor, having heard something there, does he repeat it here for the purpose of dividing those people.

Thus, he is a reconciler of those who are divided and a promoter of harmony among those who are united. Delighting in concord, rejoicing in concord, finding joy in concord, he speaks words that create concord.
This too pertains to his virtue:

having abandoned harsh speech, he abstains from harsh speech; he speaks such words as are gentle, pleasing to the ear, endearing, heart-appealing, urbane, agreeable to many people, and dear to many people.
This too pertains to his virtue.
Having abandoned idle chatter, he abstains from idle chatter; he speaks at the proper time, speaks what is true, speaks what is beneficial, speaks on the Dhamma, and speaks on the Vinaya.
He is one who utters speech that is worth treasuring—timely, grounded in reason, measured, and connected with the goal.
This too is part of his virtue.
He abstains from injuring seeds and plants...
he eats but one meal a day, refraining from eating at night and abstaining from food outside the proper time.
He abstains from dancing, singing, instrumental music, and watching spectacles.
He abstains from wearing garlands, using scents and unguents, and from adorning and beautifying himself with cosmetics.
He abstains from high and luxurious beds and seats.
He abstains from accepting gold and silver.
He abstains from accepting raw grain.
He abstains from accepting raw meat.
He abstains from accepting women and girls.
He abstains from accepting male and female slaves.
He abstains from accepting goats and sheep.
He abstains from accepting poultry and pigs.
He abstains from accepting elephants, cattle, horses, and mares.
He abstains from accepting fields and land.
He abstains from engaging in the practice of acting as a messenger or an envoy.
He abstains from buying and selling.
He abstains from cheating with false weights, false metals, and false measures.
He abstains from bribery, deception, and fraud.
He abstains from mutilating, executing, imprisoning, plundering, and using violence.
This too constitutes his virtue.
The Shorter Code of Virtue is finished.

4.3.1.2. The Intermediate Virtue Furthermore, while some venerable recluses and brahmins, having eaten food given in faith, remain devoted to such injury to the seed-plant life and the vegetable kingdom as follows:
namely, plants propagated from roots, from stems, from joints, from cuttings, and fifthly, those propagated from seeds. He abstains from such injury to the seed-plant life and the vegetable kingdom.
This too pertains to his virtue.
Or else, just as some worthy recluses and brahmins, having eaten meals given out of faith, dwell devoted to such hoarding and enjoyment, namely:
the hoarding of food, the hoarding of drink, the hoarding of clothing, the hoarding of vehicles, the hoarding of bedding, the hoarding of perfumes, and the hoarding of worldly goods.
Thus, he abstains from such forms of enjoyment involving the hoarding of goods.
This, too, is part of his virtue (*sīla*).
Furthermore, there are certain venerable recluses and brahmins who, having eaten food given in faith, remain devoted to such frivolous spectacles.
That is to say: dancing, singing, instrumental music, theatrical performances, storytelling, hand-clapping, drumming, cymbals, clowns, acrobats, mimes,
bamboo-pipe players, bath-attendants, elephant fights, horse fights, buffalo fights, bull fights,
goat fights, ram fights, cock fights, quail fights, staff-fights, and boxing matches.
He abstains from such frivolous spectacles as wrestling matches, boxing bouts, military parades, army formations, and reviews of troops;
this too is part of his virtue.
Or again, there are certain venerable recluses and brahmins who, having eaten food given in faith, remain devoted to such practices that lead to negligence through gambling.

Namely: eight-row chess, ten-row chess, *ākāsa*, *parihārapatha*, *santika*, *khalika*, *ghaṭika*, *salākahattha*, dice, *paṅgacīra*, *vaṅkaka*, *mokkhacika*, *ciṅgulika*, *pattāḷhaka*, and toy chariots.
He abstains from such games and occasions for negligence as dhanuka, akkharika, manesika, and yathāvajja, thinking "thus" or "in this way.
This too is part of his virtue.
Or again, certain venerable recluses and brahmins, having partaken of food given in faith, remain devoted to such high and luxurious beds and seats as these:
namely, a divan, a couch, a woolen rug, a variegated rug, a white woolen rug, a cotton-down quilt, a quilt of various colors,
one with long fleece on both sides, one with long fleece on one side only, a grass mat, silk, embroidered cloth, an elephant rug, a horse rug, or a chariot rug.
He abstains from such high and luxurious beds and seats as a long-haired antelope skin rug, or a rug made of the skin of a kadali deer, with a canopy above and red cushions at both ends;
this too is part of his virtue.
Or again, certain venerable recluses and brahmins, having eaten food given in faith, remain devoted to such practices of adornment and decoration as these:
namely, rubbing with unguents, massaging, bathing, shampooing, mirrors, collyrium, garlands, perfumes,
ointments, face-powder, face-cream, bracelets, topknots, staffs, flutes, swords, parasols, and variegated sandals.
He abstains from such practices as wearing a turban, a jeweled crest, or a yak-tail fan, and from using white garments with long fringes;
he refrains from such forms of adornment and decoration.
This, too, is part of his virtue.
Or again, certain venerable recluses and brahmins, having partaken of food given in faith, dwell devoted to such frivolous talk as this:
talk of kings, talk of thieves, talk of ministers, talk of armies, talk of dangers,
talk of battles, talk of food, talk of drinks, talk of clothes, talk of beds, talk of garlands, talk of perfumes, and talk of kinsmen.
He abstains from such frivolous talk as talk about vehicles, talk about villages, talk about market towns, talk about cities, talk about countries,

talk about women, talk about heroes, talk about streets, talk about wells, talk about departed ancestors, talk about various trifles, talk about the origin of the world, talk about the origin of the ocean,
or talk about "thus it was" and "thus it will be"— from such base chatter he refrains.
This also pertains to his virtue.
Or else, there are certain venerable recluses and brahmins who, having eaten meals given out of faith, dwell devoted to such contentious talk as this:
"You do not understand this Dhamma and Discipline; I understand this Dhamma and Discipline."
"How will you understand this Dhamma and Vinaya? You have practiced wrongly; I have practiced rightly.
My [practice] is consistent, yours is inconsistent. What should have been said first, you said last;
what should have been said last, you said first. Your established position has been overturned; your argument has been refuted; you are defeated. Go!"
He abstains from such contentious talk as, "Release yourself from this debate, or provide an explanation if you are able.
This too constitutes his virtue.
Furthermore, there are some venerable recluses and brahmins who, having eaten food given in faith, remain devoted to the practice of running messages and errands.
That is to say, for kings, royal ministers, kshatriyas, brahmins, householders, or princes: "Go here, go there;
take this, bring that from there"—he abstains from such practices of running messages and errands.
This too pertains to his virtue.

Or else, just as some venerable recluses and brahmins, having consumed food given in faith, become deceivers, flatterers, seekers of hints, revilers, and those who strive to obtain gain with gain. Thus...
He abstains from such hypocrisy and flattery.
This too is part of his virtue.
The middle section on virtue is concluded.
4.3.1.3. The Great Virtue (Mahāsīla).
Or again, certain venerable recluses and brahmins, having consumed food given in faith, maintain their lives by such low arts and wrong livelihood as these:
namely, [the interpretation of] body-marks, omens, portents, dreams, bodily characteristics, mouse-bitten [clothes], fire-sacrifices, and grass-sacrifices.

Thus: the burnt-offering of husks, the burnt-offering of chaff, the burnt-offering of rice grains, the burnt-offering of ghee, the burnt-offering of oil, the mouth-burnt-offering, the blood-burnt-offering;

the science of limbs, the science of sites, the science of chariots, the science of auspiciousness, the science of spirits, the science of abundance, the science of snakes, the science of poisons, the science of scorpions, the science of rats, the science of birds, the science of crows;
the meditation on cooked food, the protection from arrows, and the deer-cycle.
Thus, he abstains from such base arts and wrong livelihood as these.
This, too, is part of his virtue.
Or rather, there are certain venerable recluses and brahmins who, having consumed food given out of faith, maintain their lives through such base arts and wrong livelihood.

Namely: the characteristics of gems, the characteristics of garments, the characteristics of staffs, the characteristics of swords, the characteristics of daggers, the characteristics of spears, the characteristics of bows,
the characteristics of weapons, the characteristics of women, the characteristics of men, the characteristics of boys,

the characteristics of girls, the characteristics of male slaves, the characteristics of female slaves, the characteristics of elephants, the characteristics of horses, and the characteristics of oxen.
He abstains from such wrong livelihood as the science of omens concerning bulls, oxen, goats, rams, chickens, quails, iguanas, lizards, tortoises,
and deer; that is to say, he abstains from such low arts (tiracchānavijjā).
This too pertains to his virtue.
Or else, there are certain venerable recluses and brahmins who, having eaten meals given out of faith, maintain their lives through such base arts and wrong livelihood as these:
"There will be a military expedition for the kings; there will be no military expedition for the kings"; [or regarding] those within...
There will be the arrival of foreign kings; there will be the departure of foreign kings;
there will be the arrival of foreign kings; there will be the departure of domestic kings;
there will be victory for domestic kings; there will be defeat for foreign kings; there will be victory for foreign kings.
"Defeat will come to the internal kings; victory will belong to this one;
defeat will belong to that one"—he abstains from such base arts and wrong livelihood.
This too is part of his virtue.
Or again, certain venerable recluses and brahmins, having consumed food given in faith, maintain their lives through such base arts and wrong livelihood as these:
"There will be an eclipse of the moon; there will be an eclipse of the sun; there will be an eclipse of a constellation;
there will be the course of the sun and moon along their proper paths; there will be the course of the sun and moon along improper paths."
The stars will go on their proper courses; the stars will go astray; there will be a fall of meteors;
there will be a conflagration of the quarters; there will be an earthquake; there will be thunder from the gods;
there will be the rising, setting, defilement, and purification of the moon, the sun, and the constellations; and there will be an eclipse of the moon with such-and-such a result.
"Such will be the ripening of an eclipse of the sun; such will be the ripening of an eclipse of a constellation;
such will be the ripening of the sun and moon following their proper course; such will be the ripening of the sun and moon deviating from their proper course;
such will be the ripening of the constellations following their proper course; such will be the ripening of the constellations..."
There will be wandering onto wrong paths; such will be the ripening of the falling of meteors; such will be the ripening of the blazing of the quarters;
such will be the ripening of the earthquake; such will be the ripening of the thundering of the gods;
such will be the ripening of the rising, setting, defilement, and purification of the moon, the sun, and the constellations.
Thus, he abstains from such base arts and wrong livelihood as these.
This too is part of his virtue.
Furthermore, there are certain venerable recluses and brahmins who, having consumed food given out of faith, maintain their lives through such base arts and wrong livelihood.
Namely: there will be good rain; there will be bad rain; there will be abundance of food;
there will be scarcity of food; there will be safety; there will be danger; there will be disease; there will be health;
[and] finger-calculation, arithmetic, accounting, poetry, and cosmology.
Thus, he abstains from such base arts and wrong livelihood.
This too is part of his virtue.
For there are certain venerable recluses and brahmins who, having consumed food given in faith, maintain their lives through such base arts and wrong livelihood.
Namely: bringing together, marrying off, concealing, revealing, gathering together, scattering apart, making fortunate,
making unfortunate, causing miscarriage, binding the tongue, locking the jaw, enchanting the hand, enchanting the jaw,
enchanting the ear, the mirror-omen, the maiden-omen, the deity-omen, and the worship of the sun.
He abstains from such wrong livelihood as the practice of fortune-telling based on the Great Signs, the ritual of fire-offerings, and the invocation of the goddess Siri;
this too constitutes his virtue.
Or again, certain venerable recluses and brahmins, having consumed food given in faith, make their living by such base arts and wrong livelihood as these:
rites for propitiating deities, rites for making vows, rites for spirits, rites for the earth, rain-making rites, rites for prosperity, rites for land,
rites for preparing land, ritual rinsing, ritual bathing, burnt offerings, emetics, purgatives, and cathartics.

He abstains from such wrong livelihood as the practice of lowly arts, namely: administering purgatives, inducing vomiting, ear-oil, eye-anointing, nasal therapy, collyrium, counter-collyrium, surgery, midwifery, and the provision of medicinal roots or the extraction of herbal remedies.
Thus he refrains from such base sciences that constitute a wrong way of life.
This too belongs to his virtue.
Now, Great King, that bhikkhu, being thus perfected in virtue, perceives no fear from any quarter whatsoever, namely, regarding the restraint of virtue.
Just as, Great King, a consecrated khattiya king who has defeated his enemies perceives no fear from any quarter whatsoever, namely, from his adversaries.
In the same way, great king, a bhikkhu who is thus perfected in virtue perceives no fear from any quarter, namely, regarding the restraint of virtue.
Endowed with this noble aggregate of virtue, he experiences within himself the happiness of blamelessness.
It is in this way, great king, that a bhikkhu is perfected in virtue.
The Great Section on Virtue is finished.
4.3.2. Concentration 4.3.2.1. Restraint of the Faculties
And how, Great King, is a bhikkhu one who guards the doors of the sense faculties?
Here, Great King, a bhikkhu, having seen a form with the eye, does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary characteristics.
For, if he were to dwell with this faculty of the eye unguarded, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might arise.
Unwholesome states might flow in upon him; he practices for their restraint, guards the eye-faculty, and attains restraint over the eye-faculty.
Having heard a sound with the ear... [and so on]...
Having smelled an odor with the nose …pe… having tasted a flavor with the tongue …pe… having touched a tangible object with the body …pe…
Having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary characteristics.
Since, if he were to dwell with the faculty of the mind unrestrained, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might flow in upon him, he practices for its restraint;
he guards the faculty of the mind and achieves restraint over the faculty of the mind.
Thus, endowed with this noble restraint of the sense faculties, he experiences within himself the happiness of non-affliction.
In this way, Great King, a bhikkhu is one whose doors of the senses are guarded.
4.3.2.2. Mindfulness and Clear Comprehension (Satisampajañña)
And how, Great King, is a bhikkhu endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension?
Here, Great King, a bhikkhu acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning; he acts with clear comprehension when looking ahead and looking aside;
he acts with clear comprehension when bending and stretching his limbs; he acts with clear comprehension when wearing his outer robe, bowl, and inner robe.
He acts with clear comprehension; he acts with clear comprehension when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; he acts with clear comprehension in passing excrement and urine;
he acts with clear comprehension in going, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and remaining silent.
It is in this way, Great King, that a bhikkhu is endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension.
4.3.2.3. Contentment And how, Great King, is a bhikkhu contented?
Here, Great King, a bhikkhu is contented with robes for the body and almsfood for the belly. Wherever he goes, he goes having taken these with him.
"Just as, great king, wherever a winged bird flies, it flies with its wings as its only burden;
even so, great king, a bhikkhu is content with robes to protect his body and almsfood to sustain his belly. Wherever he goes, he goes taking only these with him.
It is in this way, great king, that a bhikkhu is content."
4.3.2.4. Abandoning the Hindrances:

Thus, being endowed with this noble aggregate of virtue, endowed with this noble restraint of the sense faculties, endowed with this noble mindfulness and clear comprehension, and endowed with this noble contentment, [he dwells].
He resorts to a secluded lodging: the forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a glen, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, an open space, or a heap of straw.
Having returned from his almsround after his meal, he sits down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him.
Abandoning covetousness for the world, he dwells with a mind free from covetousness; he purifies his mind of covetousness.
Having abandoned ill will and hatred, he dwells with a mind free from ill will, compassionate for the welfare of all living beings; he purifies his mind of ill will and hatred.
Having abandoned sloth and torpor, he dwells free from sloth and torpor, percipient of light, mindful and clearly comprehending; he purifies his mind of sloth and torpor.
Having abandoned restlessness and remorse, he dwells unagitated, with a mind inwardly tranquil; he purifies his mind of restlessness and remorse.
"Having abandoned doubt, he dwells having crossed over doubt, free from uncertainty regarding wholesome states; he purifies his mind of doubt.
Great King, it is just as if a man, having taken a loan, were to apply himself to his work, and those works of his were to succeed."
Thus, he would eliminate those old debts that were the root of his obligations, and there might remain a surplus for the maintenance of his wife.
He would think:
"In the past, I engaged in work after contracting debts."
‘My business ventures succeeded.
I cleared away my old debts and have a surplus remaining for the support of my wife.
On that account, he would find joy and experience happiness.
"It is just as if, great king, there were a man who was afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill; he would have no relish for food, nor would there be any strength in his body.
After some time, he might be freed from that affliction; he would find relish in food, and there would be strength in his body.
It would occur to him thus:"
‘Formerly, indeed, I was afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill;
food did not agree with me, and there was no strength in my body.
But now I am freed from that affliction.’
‘He provides me with food, and there is a measure of strength in my body.
On that account, he would find joy and attain happiness.
It is just as if, Great King, a man were bound in a prison.
Then, at a later time, he might be released from that prison cell in safety and security, with no loss of his wealth.
He would think to himself:
"Formerly, I was bound in a prison cell; now I am released from that prison cell in safety and security."
‘And there is no loss of any of my wealth.
On that account, he would obtain joy and attain happiness.
It is just as if, Great King, a man were a slave—not his own master, dependent on others, and unable to go where he wishes.
Then, at a later time, he might be released from that slavery, becoming his own master, independent of others, free, and able to go wherever he wishes.
It would occur to him:
"Formerly, I was a slave—dependent on others, subject to others, and unable to go wherever I wished."
‘For now I am freed from that slavery; I am my own master, independent, free, and able to go wherever I wish.
On account of this, he would find joy and attain happiness.
It is just as if, Great King, a man with wealth and property were to set out on a long journey through a wilderness, a road where food is scarce and full of dangers.
Then, at a later time, he would cross that wilderness safely and reach the edge of a village—a place secure and free from fear.
He would think to himself:
"In the past, I set out upon a journey through a wilderness road that was fraught with famine and danger, though I possessed wealth and resources."
‘For now I have crossed that wilderness safely; I have reached the edge of a village, a place secure and free from fear.
On account of this, he would obtain joy and experience happiness.
In the same way, Great King, a bhikkhu regards these five hindrances as not yet abandoned within himself, just as one regards a debt, a disease, a prison, slavery, or a journey through a wilderness.”

"Just as, great king, one regards freedom from debt, health, release from bondage, the status of a free man, or a land of safety—just so, great king, does a bhikkhu regard these five hindrances as abandoned within himself.

As he regards these five hindrances as abandoned within himself, joy arises; in one who is joyful, rapture arises; for one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil; with a tranquil body, one feels pleasure; and in one who feels pleasure, the mind becomes concentrated."
4.3.2.5. First Jhāna:

He, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.
He drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this very body with the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion; there is no part of his entire body unpervaded by the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.
"Just as, great king, a skilled bath-attendant or his apprentice,
having poured bath-powder into a bronze basin, would sprinkle it repeatedly with water and knead it, until that ball of bath-powder is permeated with oil,

saturated with oil, filled with oil both inside and out, yet does not drip; so too, great king, does this mind become concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability."
In the same way, Great King, a bhikkhu drenches, steeps, fills, and suffuses this very body with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion;
there is no part of his entire body that is not touched by the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.
This too, Great King, is a fruit of the ascetic life visible here and now, more excellent and sublime than the previous fruits of the ascetic life visible here and now.

4.3.2.6. Second Jhāna Furthermore, Great King, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal tranquility and singleness of mind, is without applied thought and without sustained thought, and possesses the rapture and happiness born of concentration.

He drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this very body with the rapture and happiness born of concentration; there is no part of his entire body that is not suffused with the rapture and happiness born of concentration.
Just as if, great king, there were a deep pool of water with its source hidden,
which had no inlet of water from the eastern direction, no inlet of water from the southern direction, no inlet of water from the western direction,
and no inlet of water from the northern direction, and the rain did not fall at regular intervals...
One might pour forth a stream of water at the right time to sustain it.
Or rather, a cool stream of water might well up from that very lake itself and completely drench,
permeate, fill, and suffuse that same lake with its cool water, so that there would be nothing in its entirety...
Just as there might be no part of a pool of water untouched by its cool water,

even so, great king, a bhikkhu drenches, steeps, fills, and suffuses this very body with the rapture and happiness born of concentration; there is no part of his entire body that is not touched by the rapture and happiness born of concentration.
This too, Great King, is a fruit of the ascetic life visible here and now, more excellent and sublime than the previous fruits of the ascetic life visible here and now.
Furthermore, Great King, with the fading away of rapture, a bhikkhu dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending.
He experiences happiness with the body, of which the Noble Ones declare: “He dwells in happiness, mindful and equanimous”;
thus he enters and dwells in the third jhāna.
He drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this very body with happiness that is free from rapture, so that there is no part of his entire body unpervaded by happiness free from rapture.
Just as, great king, in a pond of blue lotuses, or pink lotuses, or white lotuses— some of those blue, pink,
or white lotuses being born in the water, growing in the water, not rising above the water, but nourished while submerged within it—
so that from their tips down to their roots they are drenched and saturated with cool water; even so...
They were completely filled and suffused, such that there was no part of all those blue lotuses, red lotuses, or white lotuses not touched by the cool water;

even so, great king, a bhikkhu drenches, steeps, fills, and suffuses this very body with pleasure divested of rapture, so that there is no part of his entire body not touched by pleasure divested of rapture.
This too, Great King, is a fruit of the ascetic life visible here and now, more excellent and sublime than the previous fruits of the ascetic life visible here and now.
Furthermore, Great King, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna...

With the fading away of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.
He sits having pervaded this very body with a mind that is pure and bright; there is no part of his entire body unpervaded by that pure and bright mind.
Great King, it is just as if a man were sitting covered from head to foot in a white cloth, such that there would be no part of his entire body unpervaded by that white cloth.
In the same way, great king, a bhikkhu sits having pervaded this very body with a mind that is pure and bright; there is no part of his entire body unpervaded by that pure and bright mind.
This too, great king, is a fruit of the ascetic life visible here and now, more excellent and sublime than the previous fruits of the ascetic life visible here and now.
4.3.3. Eight Knowledges.

4.3.3.1. Insight-Knowledge (Vipassanāñāṇa) When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs and inclines it toward knowledge and vision.
He understands thus:

‘This body of mine is material, composed of the four great elements, born of mother and father, fed on rice and gruel, and subject to impermanence, to being rubbed and massaged, to breaking up and dissolution;
yet this consciousness of mine is dependent upon it, bound to it.
Just as if, Great King, there were a beautiful beryl gem, of pure origin, eight-faceted, well-cut, clear, translucent, unclouded, and perfect in every aspect.
There, a thread—blue, yellow, red, white, or pale gold—is strung through it.
A man with good eyesight, taking it in his hand, would examine it:
"This indeed is a beautiful beryl gem, of noble birth, eight-faceted, well-polished, clear, translucent, unclouded, and perfect in every aspect."
‘This thread is woven through it, whether blue, yellow, red, white,
or pale yellow. In the same way, Great King, when a bhikkhu’s mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished,
rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs and inclines his mind toward knowledge and vision.
Thus he understands:

"This body of mine is material, composed of the four great elements, born of mother and father, nourished by rice and gruel, and subject to impermanence, to being clothed, to being rubbed, to breaking up, and to dissolution;
yet this consciousness of mine is dependent upon it, bound to it."
“Great King, this too is a fruit of recluseship visible here and now, more excellent and sublime than the previous fruits of recluseship visible here and now.
4.3.3.2. Knowledge of the Mind-made Body:

“When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, cleansed, stainless, free from defilements, supple, wieldy, stable, and attained to imperturbability, he directs and inclines his mind toward the production of a mind-made body. He produces a mind-made body by means of his mind.”
Thus, from this body he creates another body—material, mind-made, complete in all its limbs and parts, and not lacking any faculties.
Great King, it is just as if a man were to draw a reed from a sheath of muñja grass, and it would occur to him: [“This is the sheath; this is the reed; the sheath is one thing, the reed is another”].
‘This is the reed, this is the sheath; the reed is one thing, the sheath is another; yet the sheath is drawn forth from the reed.
Or again, great king, it is as if a man were to draw a sword from its scabbard.
It would occur to him:
‘This is you, this is the sheath; you are one thing, the sheath is another, yet you are drawn out from the sheath.
Or again, Great King, it is as if a man were to pull a snake out from its skin, and he would think:
‘This is the snake, this is the basket. The snake is one thing, the basket another; yet the snake has been drawn out from the basket.

In the same way, Great King, when a bhikkhu’s mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it toward the manifestation of a mind-made body.
He directs and inclines his mind.
From this body he manifests another body—material, mind-made, complete in all its limbs and faculties, not lacking any sense organ.
This too, Great King, is a fruit of the ascetic life visible here and now, more excellent and sublime than the previous fruits of the ascetic life visible here and now.

4.3.3.3. Knowledge of the Modes of Supernormal Power (Iddhividhañāṇa) When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, cleansed, stainless, free from defilements, become supple, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs and inclines his mind toward the modes of supernormal power.
He experiences various kinds of supernormal power: having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one...
He becomes one; he appears and disappears; he passes unhindered through walls, through enclosures, and through mountains, as if through space;
he dives in and out of the earth as if it were water; he walks on water without breaking the surface as if on earth;
and he travels cross-legged through the sky like a winged bird.
He touches and strokes with his hand even these sun and moon, so powerful and majestic;
he exercises mastery with his body as far as the Brahma-world.
