Just as, Great King, a skilled potter or a potter’s apprentice might fashion and produce whatever kind of vessel he desires from well-prepared clay.
Or again, great king, just as a skilled ivory-worker, or a pupil of a skilled ivory-worker, might fashion and produce whatever ivory article he desired from well-prepared ivory;
or again, great king, just as a skilled goldsmith, or a pupil of a skilled goldsmith, might fashion and produce whatever golden article he desired from well-prepared gold.

In the same way, great king, when a bhikkhu’s mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs and inclines his mind toward the various powers of psychic transformation.
He experiences various kinds of psychic power: having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one...
He becomes one; he appears and disappears; he passes unhindered through walls, through enclosures, and through mountains, as if through space;
he dives in and out of the earth as if it were water; he walks on water without breaking the surface as if on earth;
and he travels cross-legged through the sky like a winged bird.
He touches and strokes with his hand even these sun and moon, so powerful and so majestic;
he exercises mastery with his body even as far as the Brahma-world.
This too, Great King, is a fruit of the ascetic life visible here and now, more excellent and more sublime than the previous fruits of the ascetic life visible here and now.

4.3.3.4. Divine Ear-Knowledge When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs and inclines it toward the divine ear-element.
With the divine ear-element, which is purified and surpasses the human, he hears both kinds of sounds: those of devas and those of humans, whether far or near.
“Just as if, great king, a man were traveling along a long road and should hear the sound of a kettle-drum, the sound of a tabor, and the sound of conchs, cymbals, and drums.
It would occur to him: ‘This is the sound of a kettle-drum,’ ‘this is the sound of a tabor,’ and ‘this is the sound of conchs, cymbals, and drums.’”
In the same way, great king, when a bhikkhu’s mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished,
rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs and inclines his mind toward the divine ear-element.
“With the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing that of humans, he hears both kinds of sounds—the divine and the human, whether far or near.
This too, Great King, is a fruit of the ascetic life visible here and now, more excellent and sublime than the previous fruits of the ascetic life visible here and now.
4.3.3.5. Knowledge of the Minds of Others”

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs and inclines it toward the knowledge of the minds of others.
With his own mind, he comprehends the minds of other beings and persons;
he understands a mind affected by lust as "a mind affected by lust."
He understands a mind free from lust as ‘a mind free from lust’;
he understands a mind with hatred as ‘a mind with hatred’;
he understands a mind free from hatred as ‘a mind free from hatred’.
He understands a mind with delusion as "a mind with delusion," he understands a mind free from delusion as "a mind free from delusion," and he understands a contracted mind as "a contracted mind."
Or he knows a scattered mind as "a scattered mind";
or he knows an exalted mind as "an exalted mind";
or he knows a non-exalted mind as "a non-exalted mind."
He understands a surpassed mind as ‘a surpassed mind,’ he understands an unsurpassed mind as ‘an unsurpassed mind,’ and he understands a concentrated mind as ‘a concentrated mind.’
He understands an unconcentrated mind as “an unconcentrated mind”;
he understands a liberated mind as “a liberated mind”;
and he understands an unliberated mind as “an unliberated mind.”
"Just as, great king, a woman or a man— youthful, young, and fond of adornment—
looking at the reflection of his own face in a clear, bright, and polished mirror, or in a bowl of pure water, would know it to be 'with a blemish' if it were with a blemish,
or know it to be 'without a blemish' if it were without a blemish."

In the same way, great king, when a bhikkhu’s mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs and inclines it toward the knowledge of the minds of others.

He understands the minds of other beings and persons, having encompassed them with his own mind: [The full passage continues with the various types of mental states: ...he understands a mind with lust as a mind with lust, and a mind without lust as a mind without lust; a mind with hatred as a mind with hatred, and a mind without hatred as a mind without hatred; a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion, and a mind without delusion as a mind without delusion; a contracted mind as contracted, and a distracted mind as distracted; an exalted mind as exalted, and an unexalted mind as unexalted; a surpassed mind as surpassed, and an unsurpassed mind as unsurpassed; a concentrated mind as concentrated, and an unconcentrated mind as unconcentrated; a liberated mind as liberated, and an unliberated mind as unliberated.
He understands a mind with lust as "a mind with lust," he understands a mind without lust as "a mind without lust," and he understands a mind with hatred as "a mind with hatred."
He understands a mind free from hatred as ‘a mind free from hatred’;
he understands a mind with delusion as ‘a mind with delusion’;
or he understands a mind free from delusion as ‘a mind free from delusion.’
He understands a contracted mind as "a contracted mind," he understands a distracted mind as "a distracted mind," and he understands an exalted mind as "an exalted mind."
He understands an unexalted mind as "an unexalted mind";
he understands an excelled mind as "an excelled mind";
or he understands an unsurpassed mind as "an unsurpassed mind."
He understands a concentrated mind as "a concentrated mind," he understands an unconcentrated mind as "an unconcentrated mind," and he understands a liberated mind as "a liberated mind."
Or, when the mind is unliberated, he understands: ‘The mind is unliberated.
This too, Great King, is a fruit of the ascetic life visible here and now, more excellent and sublime than the previous fruits of the ascetic life visible here and now. 4.3.3.6.
Knowledge of Recollection of Past Lives.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs and inclines it toward the knowledge of recollecting past lives.
He recollects his manifold past lives, that is to say: one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births... [and so on].
For forty births, for fifty births, for a hundred births, for a thousand births, for a hundred thousand births, for many aeons of world-contraction,
for many aeons of world-expansion, and for many aeons of both world-contraction and expansion,
[he recollects: "In that place I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan."
"Having passed away from there, I arose there; there I was with such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experiences of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan;
having passed away from there, I have reappeared here. Thus he recollects his manifold past lives in their modes and details.
"Suppose, great king, a man were to go from his own village to another village, and from that village he were to go to yet another village.
Then, returning from that village back to his own village, it would occur to him:
'I indeed went from my own village to that village; there I stood thus, sat thus, and spoke thus.'"

‘I remained silent; from that village I went to another village; there too I stood in such a way, sat in such a way, spoke in such a way, and remained silent in such a way; thus have I returned from that village to my own village.
In the same way, Great King, when a bhikkhu’s mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished—
When the mind is free from defilements, made pliant, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs and inclines it toward the knowledge of recollection of past lives.
He recollects his manifold past lives, that is to say: one birth, two births, three births... [and so on].
Whether four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births,
a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births,
or even many aeons of world-contraction, many aeons of world-expansion, and many aeons of both world-contraction and expansion— [he recollects], "In that place I was..."
‘I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a lifespan;
passing away from there, I arose elsewhere; there too I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a lifespan;
passing away from there, I was reborn here. Thus, with its aspects and particulars, he recollects his manifold past lives.
He recollects his past lives.
This too, Great King, is a fruit of the ascetic life visible here and now, more excellent and sublime than the previous fruits of the ascetic life visible here and now.
4.3.3.7. Knowledge of the Divine Eye.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs and inclines it toward the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings.

With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma: "These... [beings]..."
"Indeed, these worthy beings were possessed of misconduct in body, possessed of misconduct in speech, possessed of misconduct in mind;
they were revilers of the noble ones, held wrong views, and undertook actions based on wrong views.
With the breakup of the body, after death, they have reappeared in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell. But as for these worthy beings..."
‘These beings, endowed with good conduct of body, endowed with good conduct of speech, endowed with good conduct of mind,
not revilers of the noble ones, possessing right view, and undertaking kamma based on right view, have, with the breakup of the body, after death,
been reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world. Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans—
He sees beings passing away and being reborn—lowly and exalted, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate;
he understands how beings fare according to their own karma.
It is just as if, Great King, there were a palace in the middle of a crossroads, and a man with sight standing there were to look out.

Whether people were entering a house, leaving it, walking along a carriage road or a street, or sitting in the middle of a crossroads, it would occur to him: "These people are entering the house; these are leaving;
these are walking along the carriage road or the street; these are sitting in the middle of the crossroads."
In the same way, great king, when a bhikkhu’s mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished,
rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs and inclines it toward the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings.
Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—
inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate— and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma:
"These worthy beings, indeed, were possessed of misconduct in body, misconduct in speech, and misconduct in mind..."
These beings were possessed of wrong view, revilers of the noble ones, holders of false views, and undertakers of actions based on false views;
at the breaking up of the body, after death, they have reappeared in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, perdition, even in hell.
But these worthy beings were possessed of good conduct of body, possessed of good conduct of speech, and possessed of good conduct of mind.
‘They do not revile the noble ones, they hold right view, and they undertake actions based on right view.

With the breakup of the body, after death, they have reappeared in a good destination, a heavenly world. Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—low and high, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate.
He understands beings according to their karma.
This too, Great King, is a fruit of the ascetic life visible here and now, more excellent and sublime than the previous fruits of the ascetic life visible here and now.
4.3.3.8. Knowledge of the Destruction of the Taints.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, cleansed, stainless, free from defilements, supple, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he applies and directs his mind toward the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsava*).
He understands as it really is: "This is suffering"; he understands as it really is: "This is the origin of suffering";
he understands as it really is: "This is the cessation of suffering"; he understands as it really is: "This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering."

He understands as it really is: "These are the taints"; he understands as it really is: "This is the origin of the taints"; he understands as it really is: "This is the cessation of the taints"; he understands as it really is: "This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints.
For one who knows and sees thus, the mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, the mind is liberated from the taint of existence, and the mind is liberated from the taint of ignorance.
When liberated, the knowledge arises: "It is liberated."
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
Great King, it is just as if there were a pool of water in a mountain glen—clear, serene, and undisturbed.
A man with good eyesight standing on the bank would see the shells and snails, the pebbles and gravel, and even schools of fish.
“Whether moving or standing still. It would occur to him: ‘This pool of water is clear, serene, and undisturbed;
therein these shellfish, gravel, and pebbles, as well as schools of fish, are moving and standing still.
In the same way, Great King, when a bhikkhu’s mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, and free from blemish...”
When the mind is free from corruptions, pliant, workable, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs and inclines it toward the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.
He understands as it really is: "This is suffering"; he understands as it really is: "This is the origin of suffering."
One understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; one understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
One understands as it really is: ‘These are the taints’; one understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of the taints.’
He understands as it really is: “This is the cessation of the taints”; he understands as it really is: “This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints.
For one who thus knows and thus sees, the mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, the mind is liberated from the taint of existence, and the mind is liberated from the taint of ignorance.
When liberated, the knowledge arises: "It is liberated.
One understands: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
This, Great King, is the fruit of recluseship visible here and now, which is more excellent and more sublime than the previous fruits of recluseship visible here and now.
“Moreover, Great King, there is no other fruit of recluseship more visible, higher, or more sublime than this fruit of recluseship.
When this was said, the Magadhan King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta said this to the Blessed One:
“Excellent, Bhante! Excellent, Bhante!

Just as, Bhante, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—[so has the Dhamma been made clear by the Blessed One].”
"Even so, Bhante, has the Dhamma been proclaimed by the Blessed One in many ways.
Venerable sir, I go for refuge to the Blessed One, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last."

“Venerable sir, a transgression has overcome me—like that of a fool, like that of one who is deluded, like that of one who is unwholesome—in that for the sake of sovereignty, I deprived my father, a righteous king of Dhamma, of life.
Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept my transgression as a transgression, for the sake of future restraint.

“Truly, great king, a transgression has overcome you—like that of a fool, like that of one who is deluded, like that of one who is unwholesome—in that you deprived your father, a righteous king of Dhamma, of life.”
"But since you, Great King, having seen your transgression as a transgression, make amends for it in accordance with the Dhamma, we accept it from you.

For this, Great King, is growth in the discipline of the Noble One: that one who sees a transgression as a transgression makes amends for it in accordance with the Dhamma and undertakes restraint for the future.
When this was said, Ajātasattu Vedehiputta, the King of Magadha, said this to the Blessed One:
“Now, venerable sir, we must go; we have many duties and much to do.
“Do as you think fit, great king,” the Blessed One replied.

Then King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha, having rejoiced and expressed his appreciation for the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed.
Then, not long after King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha had departed, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, this king has been ruined;
bhikkhus, this king has been destroyed.”
“Bhikkhus, if you were not to deprive this righteous father, the Dhamma-king, of life, then even on this very seat, the dustless, stainless Eye of Dhamma would arise.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Elated, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The Discourse on the Fruits of the Ascetic Life is finished; this is the second.
